---
title: "Finding paragraph boundaries"
subtitle: "Keep layout units before text conversion removes them"
description: "Learn how blank lines and HTML block elements mark paragraphs in different file formats."
categories: [sentences and paragraphs, paragraph segmentation, workforce research]
---

Help articles and job-board HTML store paragraph boundaries differently. The
coordinator needs to preserve those boundaries before text cleanup removes
them.

In a plain-text help article, a blank line can mark a new paragraph. HTML gives
the team block elements for paragraph boundaries. The HTML standard does not
restrict its paragraph definition to `<p>` elements. This lesson therefore
uses a working rule rather than the specification's full definition.

::: {.callout-note}
The help articles and job board are local fictional fixtures.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## What you will learn

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

- explain a paragraph as a layout unit.
- split plain text on blank lines.
- collect paragraph-like blocks from HTML with rvest.
- compare paragraph counts across file formats.
- explain why extraction must preserve block boundaries before tag removal.
:::

```{r}
#| include: false

options(warn = 2)
stopifnot(identical(getOption("warn"), 2L))
```

## Split plain text on blank lines

readr reads files, while purrr applies the same operations across files.
stringr splits text, and tidyr expands list columns. dplyr and tibble prepare
tables, and rvest reads HTML. A **paragraph** is a block of text grouped by
layout. It may contain one sentence or several.

```{r}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tibble)
library(purrr)
library(stringr)
library(tidyr)
library(rvest)

help_files <- list.files(
  "data/help_articles",
  pattern = "[.]txt$",
  full.names = TRUE
) |>
  sort()

split_blank_lines <- function(text) {
  str_split(str_trim(text), "\\r?\\n\\s*\\r?\\n+")[[1]] |>
    str_trim() |>
    discard(\(piece) identical(piece, ""))
}

help_articles <- tibble(
  file = basename(help_files),
  text = map_chr(help_files, read_file)
) |>
  mutate(paragraph = map(text, split_blank_lines))

help_paragraphs <- help_articles |>
  select(file, paragraph) |>
  unnest_longer(paragraph) |>
  group_by(file) |>
  mutate(paragraph_number = row_number()) |>
  ungroup()

help_counts <- help_paragraphs |>
  count(file, name = "paragraphs")

total_help_paragraphs <- sum(help_counts$paragraphs)
help_blank_line_counts <- str_count(help_articles$text, "\\r?\\n\\s*\\r?\\n+")
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  help_counts,
  col.names = c("Help article", "Paragraphs from blank-line rule"),
  caption = "Paragraph counts in the plain-text help articles",
  row.names = FALSE
)

knitr::kable(
  help_paragraphs,
  col.names = c("Help article", "Paragraph", "Paragraph number"),
  caption = "Plain-text paragraphs after splitting on blank lines",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(all(c(
  "readr", "dplyr", "tibble", "purrr", "stringr", "tidyr", "rvest"
) %in% loadedNamespaces()))

stopifnot(
  identical(length(help_files), 3L),
  identical(help_counts$paragraphs, c(1L, 1L, 1L)),
  identical(total_help_paragraphs, 3L),
  identical(help_blank_line_counts, c(0L, 0L, 0L)),
  str_detect(help_paragraphs$paragraph[1], fixed("password reset link"))
)
```

None of these help files contains a blank line. The rule therefore returns
each complete file without demonstrating a split. The HTML example requires
an explicit choice of boundary rule.

## Take blocks from HTML

HTML records layout with elements. The code below reads the job-board page and
keeps headings, paragraphs, and list items. The selector `h1, h2, p, li` names
the block types the team wants to treat as paragraph-like units.

```{r}
job_page <- read_html("data/workforce/job-board.html")
block_nodes <- html_elements(job_page, "h1, h2, p, li")

html_blocks <- tibble(
  tag = html_name(block_nodes),
  text = html_text2(block_nodes)
) |>
  mutate(block_number = row_number())

html_tag_counts <- html_blocks |>
  count(tag, name = "blocks") |>
  arrange(tag)

expected_tag_counts <- tibble(
  tag = c("h1", "h2", "li", "p"),
  blocks = c(1L, 6L, 22L, 12L)
)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  html_tag_counts,
  col.names = c("HTML tag", "Blocks captured"),
  caption = "Paragraph-like blocks captured from the job-board HTML",
  row.names = FALSE
)

knitr::kable(
  html_blocks |>
    slice_head(n = 8),
  col.names = c("HTML tag", "Text", "Block number"),
  caption = "The first eight block elements from the job board",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(nrow(html_blocks), 41L),
  identical(html_tag_counts, expected_tag_counts),
  identical(html_blocks$text[1], "Riverton workforce opportunities"),
  identical(html_blocks$text[5], "Paid 12-week training is provided."),
  identical(sum(html_blocks$tag == "li"), 22L)
)
```

The HTML rule finds 41 blocks: 1 page heading, 6 job headings, 12 paragraph
elements, and 22 list items. The job-detail sentences in the Riverton CSV came
from those list items.

## Show what tag removal loses

A common conversion removes tags and retains visible words. This operation
can help word counting, but it also removes the markers needed for paragraph
segmentation.

```{r}
html_source <- read_file("data/workforce/job-board.html")
stripped_before_squish <- html_source |>
  str_remove_all("<[^>]+>")

paragraphs_after_tag_removal <- split_blank_lines(stripped_before_squish)
paragraphs_after_squish <- stripped_before_squish |>
  str_squish() |>
  split_blank_lines()

boundary_loss <- tibble(
  source = c(
    "HTML block elements",
    "Tags removed, whitespace preserved",
    "Tags removed, whitespace squished"
  ),
  paragraph_like_units = c(
    nrow(html_blocks),
    length(paragraphs_after_tag_removal),
    length(paragraphs_after_squish)
  )
)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  boundary_loss,
  col.names = c("Rule", "Paragraph-like units"),
  caption = "Whitespace cleanup collapses the tag-stripped text",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(length(paragraphs_after_tag_removal), 14L),
  identical(length(paragraphs_after_squish), 1L),
  identical(boundary_loss$paragraph_like_units, c(41L, 14L, 1L)),
  str_starts(paragraphs_after_squish[1], "Riverton workforce opportunities"),
  str_ends(paragraphs_after_squish[1], "Clear written communication is an essential skill.")
)
```

Tag removal alone leaves 14 blank-line chunks because the source file still has
line breaks and indentation. Those chunks reflect source layout around
titles, job cards, and lists rather than paragraphs. `str_squish()` removes the remaining
blank-line boundaries and leaves one long text string. For this file, paragraph
segmentation must preserve structure before whitespace cleanup.

## What to remember

- A paragraph is a layout block, so the right rule depends on the file format.
- These help files have no blank lines, so the blank-line rule cannot show much.
- The chosen HTML selector captures 41 block-like units. Those units contain
  headings and list items.
- Squishing whitespace after tag removal collapses the text to one unit.

The help files and the job-board HTML need different boundary rules. Here the
reported counts are layout counts, not a grammar claim about where paragraphs
must begin.
